fetched_contents.text: A Novel Carbon Monoxide-Releasing Molecule Fully Protects Mice from Severe Malaria Abstract Severe forms of malaria infection, such as cerebral malaria (CM) and acute lung injury (ALI), are mainly caused by the apicomplexan parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Primary therapy with quinine or artemisinin derivatives is generally effective in controlling P. falciparum parasitemia, but mortality from CM and other forms of severe malaria remains unacceptably high. Herein, we report the design and synthesis of a novel carbon monoxide-releasing molecule (CO-RM; ALF492) that fully protects mice against experimental CM (ECM) and ALI. ALF492 enables controlled CO delivery in vivo without affecting oxygen transport by hemoglobin, the major limitation in CO inhalation therapy. The protective effect is CO dependent and induces the expression of heme oxygenase-1, which contributes to the observed protection. Importantly, when used in combination with the antimalarial drug artesunate, ALF492 is an effective adjunctive and adjuvant treatment for ECM, conferring protection after the onset of severe disease. This study paves the way for the potential use of CO-RMs, such as ALF492, as adjunctive/adjuvant treatment in severe forms of malaria infection. INTRODUCTION Malaria remains a devastating global health problem, resulting in up to 800,000 annual deaths (29, 34, 39, 46). Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe forms of malaria infection, such as cerebral malaria (CM) and acute lung injury (ALI) (41). The case-fatality rate in severe malaria treated with either artemisinin or quinine derivatives remains unacceptably high; CM is among the deadliest syndromes, with 13 to 21% mortality, even after antimalarial treatment (19). In an effort to reduce malaria-related mortality, numerous adjunctive/adjuvant therapies complementing treatment to an antimalarial therapy have been suggested and tested (21). However, to date, there is still no effective adjunctive/adjuvant therapy for severe malaria. Animal models have been an indispensable tool for malaria immunopathogenesis research, drug testing, and vaccine development. Various mouse-parasite combinations can lead to different malaria-associated syndromes. In particular, P. berghei ANKA strain can induce in rodents distinct malaria pathologies, such as cerebral malaria and acute lung injury (11, 32). The relevance of these models to understanding of human malaria has been questioned due to some differences in clinical features between human and mouse severe malaria, particularly in cerebral malaria. While these models individually may not reflect all the features of specific syndromes, globally they have been crucial to understanding the pathogenesis of severe malaria (13, 23). Using the P. berghei ANKA cerebral malaria model, we have shown that heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) is a key protective gene against the development of CM in mice. Moreover, inhalation of carbon monoxide (CO), one of the end products of HO-1 activity, fully prevented CM and malaria-associated ALI (M-AALI) incidence in C57BL/6 mice (11, 32). Research conducted in other experimental models has further shown that HO-1/CO display cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties that are beneficial for the resolution of acute inflammation (17, 24). CO holds great promise as a therapeutic agent (28, 36). However, the safety and practicability of the application of CO gas in the clinic remain questionable due to its toxicity and the need for highly controlled medical facilities. Thus, CO-releasing molecules (CO-RMs) have been put forward as a valid alternative to CO gas (reviewed in references 28 and 36). Among the early-developed and still widely used CO-RMs in experimental models are the lipid-soluble CORM-2 [Ru(CO)3Cl2]2 and the water-soluble CORM-3 [Ru(CO)3Cl2(H2NCH2CO)2] models. Neither CORM-2 nor CORM-3 elevates carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) levels in blood after in vivo administration (9). Most importantly, substantial protective effects similar to those observed for CO inhalation have been reported using these CO-RMs in various experimental models of disease, such as bacterial infection, vascular dysfunction, and thermal and ischemia-reperfusion injury (1, 9, 22). These CO-RMs lack some key drug-like properties, including adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration, but serve as a proof of concept and offer a safer and more efficient modality to deliver CO than CO gas administration. Building upon this knowledge, we report the design and synthesis of a novel CO-RM (ALF492) that displays improved water solubility, is able to transfer CO to heme proteins, does not induce the formation of measurable levels of COHb, and distributes in vivo with a significant affinity for the liver. The bioactivity and key therapeutic features of ALF492 are shown in two distinct models of severe malaria. Importantly, our data show the use of this compound as a promising adjunctive/adjuvant therapy during the acute phase of cerebral malaria. MATERIALS AND METHODS Reagents. CORM-3, fac-Ru(CO)3Cl(NH2CH2COO) or fac-Ru(CO)3Cl(glycinate), was synthesized as described previously (9), and ALF466 [tetrakis(dimethyl sulfoxide)dichlororuthenium(II)] and tricarbonyldichlororuthenium(II) dimer (CORM-2) were purchased from Strem Chemicals, Inc., and Sigma-Aldrich, respectively. β-d-Thiogalactopyranoside was purchased from Carbosynth. fetched_contents.text: Heme oxygenase-1, carbon monoxide, and malaria – The interplay of chemistry and biology Highlights * • Heme exerts cytotoxic effects that can lead to inflammation. * • HO-1 degrades heme and affects resistance and susceptibility to infection. * • Heme/HO-1/CO impacts the pathogenesis and outcomes of experimental severe malaria. * • CO-releasing molecules are therapeutic candidates for malaria and other diseases. Abstract Transition metals, including iron, are central to the chemistry of life, bridging inorganic chemistry and biology and playing various biochemical roles. Endogenous and biologically active ‘gases’ including NO and CO, have the remarkable ability to bind metal centers making metalloproteins and, in particular, hemoproteins one of its most common targets. Heme, an iron-centered porphyrin, is a metal prosthetic group present in various metalloproteins, including hemoglobin. Heme oxygenases are the enzymes responsible for the catabolism of heme through a unique mechanism where heme is utilized both as substrate and cofactor. Heme oxygenases play critical roles in heme homeostasis, iron recycling, and response to stress and inflammation, particularly HO-1, its inducible form. HO-1 and its by-products — biliverdin, CO, and iron — have documented antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immunoregulatory roles. However, during infection, HO-1 may contribute to limiting pathogen burden and prevent host damage or promote pathogen growth and infection. Malaria was one of the first infectious diseases where these two facets of HO-1 were uncovered. In models of severe malaria, HO-1 was shown to play essential roles in controlling resistance and susceptibility to experimental cerebral malaria and malaria-associated acute lung injury via the production of CO. These and other studies have supported CO as a promising therapeutic agent for a range of inflammatory conditions. However, the use of CO gas in the clinic remains questionable due to safety concerns. The emergence of CO-releasing molecules, mostly organometallic carbonyl complexes capable of delivering CO to cells and tissues in a controlled fashion, have been considered a valid alternative to CO inhalation. This review focuses on the heme/HO-1/CO pathway and its role in infectious diseases, particularly severe malaria. We also address current knowledge on the crosstalk between NO and HO-1/CO and its impact on severe malaria susceptibility. Finally, we discuss the use of CO-releasing molecules as a feasible therapeutic strategy for severe malaria and other diseases. The field of bioinorganic chemistry studies the biological role of metal ions, the structure and function of metalloproteins, and metal ion homeostasis in health and disease. In particular, medicinal inorganic chemistry explores the development of metal-based compounds as therapeutic and diagnostic agents for human disease [1]. Several transition metals, including iron (Fe), zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), manganese (Mn), molybdenum (Mo), tungsten (W), nickel (Ni), cobalt (Co), chromium (Cr), vanadium (V), are essential components of metalloproteins and play critical roles in the chemistry of living systems [1], [3], [4]. Metalloproteins comprise between 40% and 50% of all identified proteins [5]. The metal ions contained in these proteins participate in a diversity of biochemical roles, serving as cofactors, structural components, mediators of electron transfer in redox reactions, or signaling processes [4], [5], [6], [7]. Among all transition metals, iron is the most predominant metal ion in biological systems. Under physiological conditions, iron exists mainly in two redox states, the reduced ferrous (Fe2+) and the oxidized ferric (Fe3+), which are interchangeable. Due to the redox potential of Fe2+/Fe3+, iron is extremely versatile when incorporated into proteins as a catalytic center or as an electron carrier [8]. In mammalian cells, iron is required mainly for the biosynthesis of heme and the biogenesis of iron-sulfur clusters, which are ubiquitous prosthetic groups essential for a plethora of proteins [9], [10]. Heme-containing proteins, also known as hemoproteins, are vital for several diverse physiological processes, such as dioxygen transport and storage, catalysis, and gas sensing [6]. In mammals, heme — a ferrous iron (Fe2+) tetrapyrrole protoporphyrin IX complex with a high affinity for oxygen — is an essential prosthetic group of several hemoproteins with major functions in cellular physiology and metabolism (e.g., hemoglobin (Hb), myoglobin, cytochromes, catalases, peroxidases, and nitric oxide synthase (NOS) enzymes [8]. How CO and CORM chemistry and dosing shape their utility

The utility of CO and CORMs in experimental cerebral malaria is heavily shaped by their chemical design, dosing strategy, and formulation. First, CO itself is a gasotransmitter with limited bioavailability and delivery constraints, whereas CORMs are designed to overcome these by delivering CO in a controlled, localized fashion. The N1 evidence emphasizes that CO-RMs such as ALF492 enable controlled CO delivery in vivo without affecting oxygen transport by hemoglobin, a major limitation of CO inhalation therapy [N1-F1]. This chemical advantage makes CORMs more suitable for therapeutic use than gaseous CO, which is unsafe and impractical for clinical application [N1-F1].

Chemical properties also determine release and targeting. The N2 review highlights that CO-releasing molecules, mostly organometallic carbonyl complexes, are therapeutic candidates because they can deliver CO to cells and tissues in a controlled fashion [N2-F2]. The N1 study further reports that ALF492 is a novel CO-RM with improved water solubility, the ability to transfer CO to heme proteins, and a significant liver affinity in vivo [N1-F1]. These formulation differences are important because they affect bioavailability, stability, and tissue distribution after administration. In contrast, older CO-RMs like CORM-2 and CORM-3 have been noted to lack adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution, though they still serve as proof of concept [N1-F1]. This suggests that formulation improvements can enhance both safety and efficacy.

Dosing routes and timing are also central. The N4 evidence includes examples of malaria treatment strategies such as splitting a dose of 20 mg/kg artemisinin every 24 hours into two 10 mg/kg doses every 12 hours, which was highly effective [N4-R1]. While this is not directly about CO or CORMs, it illustrates the importance of dosing schedules in malaria therapy and implies that timing can influence effectiveness. The N5 evidence similarly notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids in inflammatory suppression [N5-R1], suggesting that dosing timing and combination may matter in adjunctive therapy. For CO and CORMs, the N1 evidence explicitly states that ALF492 was used as an effective adjunctive and adjuvant treatment for ECM after the onset of severe disease [N1-F1]. This indicates that dosing after disease onset may be a key consideration in malaria therapy.

Formulation differences can change safety and efficacy profiles. The N3 evidence notes that preclinical and clinical data suggest low concentrations of gaseous CO or synthetic CORMs may mitigate cellular damage, but also highlights the broader toxicity concerns associated with CO poisoning [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The N1 evidence specifically emphasizes that ALF492 does not induce measurable COHb levels in blood after in vivo administration and distributes with a significant liver affinity [N1-F1]. This formulation distinction reduces some of the limitations of CO gas and may improve safety. However, the N3 evidence also reminds us that CO poisoning can have serious clinical consequences, ranging from headache and dizziness to coma and death [N3-R2]. This means that even with CORMs, safety remains a concern and formulation differences can still influence toxicity.

Overall, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: CO and CORMs are useful because they can deliver CO in a more controlled and tissue-targeted way than gas inhalation, but their utility depends critically on chemical design, dosing route, timing, and formulation, with formulation differences able to improve safety and efficacy while still leaving toxicity risks intact [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2].

What advantages CO and CORMs offer in experimental cerebral malaria

The advantages of CO and CORMs in experimental cerebral malaria are primarily mechanistic and clinical. First, they show specific anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects. The N1 evidence reports that ALF492 induces HO-1 expression and that this is associated with protection in experimental cerebral malaria [N1-F1]. The N2 review likewise states that HO-1 and CO have documented antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immunoregulatory roles and that CO-releasing molecules are therapeutic candidates for malaria and other diseases [N2-F2]. The N2-R4 excerpt adds that both HO-1 and CO prevented blood-brain barrier disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation, including CD8+ effects [N2-R4]. This mechanistic evidence supports the idea that CO and CORMs act through anti-inflammatory pathways rather than simply killing parasites.

Second, they can improve clinical outcomes. The N1 evidence states that ALF492 fully protected mice against experimental cerebral malaria and acute lung injury, and that it was effective as an adjunctive and adjuvant treatment for ECM after the onset of severe disease [N1-F1]. The same study also notes that the protective effect was CO dependent [N1-F1]. The N1-R5 excerpt reinforces this by stating that neither HO-1 nor CO affected parasitemia, but both prevented BBB disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation [N1-R5]. This implies that the main benefit in malaria models is not necessarily reduced parasite burden, but reduced neurological and vascular damage, which is especially relevant in cerebral malaria. The N5 evidence also notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids in suppressing inflammatory effects [N5-R1], suggesting a role in augmenting conventional anti-inflammatory therapy.

Third, the evidence suggests potential advantages over conventional adjunctive therapies in the context of cerebral malaria. The N1 study explicitly frames CO-RMs as adjunctive/adjuvant treatment for severe malaria infection and notes that they may be useful during the acute phase of cerebral malaria [N1-F1]. The N5 evidence adds that CO has been highlighted as a potential therapeutic agent with anti-inflammatory properties and that metal-based CORMs are emerging for their striking anti-inflammatory properties [N5-R4][N5-R3]. In comparison, conventional adjunctive therapies such as corticosteroids are being considered for inflammation suppression, but CO appears to potentiate their effects [N5-R1]. This suggests that CO and CORMs may complement rather than replace standard therapies, and that their anti-inflammatory profile could be especially valuable in cerebral malaria, where neuroinflammation and BBB disruption are major pathologic features [N2-R4][N1-F1].

Taken together, the evidence indicates that CO and CORMs offer advantages in experimental cerebral malaria by acting through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory mechanisms, by reducing BBB disruption and neuroinflammation, and by showing efficacy as adjunctive therapy in severe disease [N1-F1][N2-F2][N2-R4][N1-R5]. However, the evidence also leaves room for caution: the protection is CO dependent and the models used may not fully reflect human cerebral malaria [N1-F1].

What limitations and risks CO and CORMs pose in experimental cerebral malaria

The limitations and risks of CO and CORMs in experimental cerebral malaria include toxicity, oxidative stress, off-target effects, dose-dependent adverse effects, and translation barriers such as delivery, stability, and pharmacokinetics. The N3 evidence is especially important here, because it notes that preclinical and clinical data even suggest low concentrations of gaseous CO or synthetic CORMs may mitigate cellular damage, but it also highlights the broader toxicity concerns associated with CO poisoning [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The N3-R2 excerpt states that clinical presentation in CO poisoning ranges from headache and dizziness to coma and death [N3-R2], which underscores the safety concern even when CO is used at low concentrations. The N3-R3 excerpt also emphasizes that CO poisoning is a leading cause of fatal poisoning worldwide [N3-R3], reinforcing the need for careful dosing and formulation.

Toxicity and oxidative stress are particularly relevant. The N3 evidence indicates that CO toxicity is a major concern, but it does not directly specify oxidative stress as a mechanism in malaria models. Still, the broader toxicological context is clear: CO is a poison, and its use in the clinic remains questionable due to safety concerns [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The N1 evidence also notes that the protective effect of ALF492 was CO dependent, which implies that CO itself has biological activity that can be harmful at the wrong dose or route [N1-F1]. This means that the same molecule that can be beneficial can also be toxic if not carefully controlled.

Dose-dependent adverse effects and variability across species or models are also evident. The N1 evidence states that substantial protective effects similar to CO inhalation have been reported using CORMs, but that these CO-RMs lack some key drug-like properties, including adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration [N1-F1]. This formulation variability suggests that efficacy and safety may depend on dosing and model-specific responses. The N4 evidence provides an example of dose splitting in malaria treatment, showing that splitting a 20 mg/kg dose into two 10 mg/kg doses every 12 hours was highly effective [N4-R1]. While this is not CO-specific, it illustrates how dosing timing can matter and implies that different models or species may respond differently to CO or CORM exposure [N4-R1]. The N5 evidence also notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids, which suggests that the interaction between dose, timing, and adjunctive therapy can change the overall effect [N5-R1].

Barriers to translation include delivery, stability, and pharmacokinetics. The N1 evidence explicitly states that CO-RMs such as ALF492 were developed because CO gas therapy is unsafe and requires highly controlled medical facilities [N1-F1]. It also notes that older CO-RMs such as CORM-2 and CORM-3 lack adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration [N1-F1]. The N3 evidence further supports the broader issue of toxicity and delivery, because CO is a gas that is difficult to administer safely [N3-R1][N3-R2]. These factors make translation from preclinical to clinical use challenging, even though CORMs offer a more practical delivery modality than CO gas.

In summary, the evidence suggests that CO and CORMs pose limitations and risks primarily because of toxicity and safety concerns, dose-dependent adverse effects, and formulation issues such as solubility, stability, and tissue distribution [N3-R1][N3-R2][N1-F1]. These limitations make translation difficult and highlight why careful dosing, formulation, and model selection are essential [N4-R1][N5-R1].

Malaria-specific mechanisms and disease tolerance roles of CO and CORMs

CO and CORMs appear to play a malaria-specific role through the heme/HO-1/CO pathway and disease tolerance mechanisms, rather than through direct antiparasitic activity. The N2 review is central here: it states that heme oxygenase-1, carbon monoxide, and malaria are the focus, and that the heme/HO-1/CO pathway impacts the pathogenesis and outcomes of experimental severe malaria [N2-R1][N2-F2]. It also notes that HO-1 degrades heme and affects resistance and susceptibility to infection, and that heme can exert cytotoxic effects that lead to inflammation [N2-F2]. This establishes the broader biological context for malaria-specific effects.

The evidence supports a disease tolerance rather than direct antiparasitic mechanism. The N1 evidence reports that neither HO-1 nor CO affected parasitemia in experimental cerebral malaria, but both prevented BBB disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation [N1-R5]. The N2-R4 excerpt adds that HO-1 and CO prevented BBB disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation, including CD8+ effects [N2-R4]. The N4-R2 evidence, while not malaria-specific, illustrates that intranasal drug delivery can be used in malaria models, suggesting that the malaria-specific mechanism is biological rather than delivery-dependent [N4-R2]. Together, these sources suggest that CO and CORMs mainly protect by reducing inflammation and BBB damage rather than by directly killing parasites.

The disease tolerance role is further supported by the N6 evidence. The N6-R1 excerpt states that HO-1 is an inducible enzyme involved in heme degradation and has been demonstrated to play a crucial role in the host's response to Plasmodium [N6-R1]. The N6-R3 excerpt explains that heme catabolism by HO-1 produces CO, which prevents further heme release from cell-free hemoglobin after Plasmodium infection and suppresses disease [N6-R3]. The N6-R4 excerpt reinforces that sickle hemoglobin confers tolerance to Plasmodium infection [N6-R4], supporting the broader idea that host mechanisms can tolerate malaria rather than simply eliminate parasites. The N6-R2 excerpt also describes a mechanism of host defense based on tissue cytoprotection against free heme and limiting disease severity [N6-R2]. These findings fit with the idea that CO and CORMs are part of a disease tolerance pathway that limits host damage while the infection persists [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4].

The evidence also points to effects on BBB disruption, neuroinflammation, and brain microvasculature. The N2-R4 excerpt explicitly states that HO-1 and CO prevented BBB disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation [N2-R4]. The N1-R5 excerpt similarly reports that neither HO-1 nor CO affected parasitemia, but both prevented BBB disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation [N1-R5]. This is especially important in cerebral malaria, where BBB breakdown and neuroinflammation are major drivers of disease severity. The N2 review also notes that HO-1/CO display cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties beneficial for the resolution of acute inflammation [N2-F2], which is relevant to the brain microvasculature and neuroinflammation in malaria.

In conclusion, the evidence supports a malaria-specific mechanism in which CO and CORMs operate through the heme/HO-1/CO pathway and disease tolerance, reducing BBB disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation [N2-R1][N2-R4][N1-R5]. The evidence also suggests that the main effect is anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective rather than direct antiparasitic [N1-R5][N6-R3]. This distinction is important because it suggests that CO and CORMs may be more useful as adjunctive therapies in cerebral malaria than as direct antimalarial agents [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Integrated final answer: advantages and limitations of CO and CORM adjunctive therapies in experimental cerebral malaria

Carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon monoxide-releasing molecules (CORMs) are increasingly viewed as promising adjunctive therapies in experimental cerebral malaria, but their utility is shaped by a balance of biological advantages, practical limitations, and translation barriers. The evidence from the four upstream branches points to a consistent picture: CO and CORMs are most attractive as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents rather than as direct antiparasitic treatments, and they can improve outcomes in severe malaria by protecting against neurological damage and BBB disruption. At the same time, they carry safety concerns, dose-dependent risks, and formulation-related barriers that make their clinical translation challenging [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2][N5-R1].

---

### 1) Key advantages of CO and CORMs in experimental cerebral malaria

The main advantages are mechanistic and clinical, centered on anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects.

#### a) Specific anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects
The evidence shows that CO and CORMs act through a pathway that includes heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and CO production, with documented antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immunoregulatory roles [N2-F2]. In malaria models, this pathway is especially relevant because HO-1 degrades heme and affects resistance and susceptibility to infection, while heme can exert cytotoxic effects that lead to inflammation [N2-F2]. The N1 evidence also reports that ALF492 induces HO-1 expression and that this is associated with protection in experimental cerebral malaria [N1-F1]. This is important because it suggests that CO and CORMs are not merely bystanders in malaria; they are part of a host response that actively modulates inflammation [N2-R4][N1-F1].

#### b) Improvements in clinical outcomes
The most direct clinical evidence comes from experimental cerebral malaria models. The N1 study reports that ALF492 fully protected mice against experimental cerebral malaria and acute lung injury, and that it was effective as an adjunctive and adjuvant treatment for ECM after the onset of severe disease [N1-F1]. It also found that neither HO-1 nor CO affected parasitemia, but both prevented blood-brain barrier disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation [N1-R5]. This is a critical distinction: the main benefit in malaria models appears to be reduced BBB damage and neuroinflammation, rather than lower parasite burden [N1-F1][N1-R5]. In cerebral malaria, where neurological damage is a major determinant of severity and outcome, this is a substantial advantage [N2-R4].

#### c) Potential advantages over conventional adjunctive therapies
CO and CORMs may complement rather than replace standard adjunctive therapies. The N5 evidence notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids in suppressing inflammatory effects [N5-R1], suggesting a role in augmenting conventional anti-inflammatory therapy. It also states that CO has been highlighted as a potential therapeutic agent with anti-inflammatory properties and that metal-based CORMs are emerging for their striking anti-inflammatory properties [N5-R4][N5-R3]. In that sense, CO and CORMs appear to be particularly attractive in cerebral malaria, where inflammation and BBB disruption are central pathologic features [N5-R1][N2-R4].

Overall, the advantages of CO and CORMs are best summarized as: they can reduce inflammation, protect the brain and vasculature, and may work as effective adjuncts in severe malaria, especially when administered after disease onset [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R1].

---

### 2) Major limitations and risks of CO and CORMs in experimental cerebral malaria

Despite these advantages, CO and CORMs are not without serious limitations and risks.

#### a) Toxicity and safety concerns
CO itself is a poison, and CO poisoning can have serious clinical consequences ranging from headache and dizziness to coma and death [N3-R2]. The N3 evidence also notes that preclinical and clinical data suggest low concentrations of gaseous CO or synthetic CORMs may mitigate cellular damage, but it also highlights the broader toxicity concerns associated with CO poisoning [N3-R1][N3-R2]. This is a major limitation because it means that even if CO is beneficial in malaria, its use must be carefully controlled to avoid systemic toxicity [N3-R2].

#### b) Dose-dependent adverse effects and variability across species or models
The evidence suggests that efficacy and safety are dose-dependent. The N1 study notes that substantial protective effects similar to CO inhalation have been reported using CORMs, but that these CO-RMs lack some key drug-like properties, including adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration [N1-F1]. The N4 evidence provides an example of dose splitting in malaria treatment, showing that splitting a 20 mg/kg dose into two 10 mg/kg doses every 12 hours was highly effective [N4-R1]. While this is not CO-specific, it illustrates the importance of timing and dosing in malaria therapy and implies that different models or species may respond differently to CO or CORM exposure [N4-R1]. The N5 evidence also notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids, which suggests that the interaction between dose, timing, and adjunctive therapy can change the overall effect [N5-R1].

#### c) Barriers to translation: delivery, stability, and pharmacokinetics
One of the major barriers to clinical translation is that CO gas therapy remains unsafe and requires highly controlled medical facilities [N1-F1]. CORMs were developed precisely to overcome this limitation by delivering CO in a controlled, localized way [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, older CO-RMs such as CORM-2 and CORM-3 have been noted to lack adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration [N1-F1]. This means that formulation differences can significantly affect whether a CORM behaves like a useful therapeutic or a problematic compound [N1-F1]. The N3 evidence also reinforces the broader safety concern by emphasizing that CO poisoning can be fatal [N3-R3].

In short, the limitations are: toxicity, dose dependence, formulation instability, and the challenge of translating a gas-based therapy into a safe and practical clinical intervention [N3-R2][N1-F1][N4-R1].

---

### 3) How CO and CORM chemistry and dosing shape their utility

The utility of CO and CORMs is strongly shaped by their chemistry, dosing strategy, and formulation.

#### a) Chemical properties affecting bioavailability and release
CO itself is a gasotransmitter with limited bioavailability and delivery constraints, whereas CORMs are designed to overcome these by delivering CO in a controlled, localized fashion [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The N2 review explains that CO-releasing molecules, mostly organometallic carbonyl complexes, are therapeutic candidates because they can deliver CO to cells and tissues in a controlled fashion [N2-F2]. The N1 evidence reports that ALF492 is a novel CO-RM with improved water solubility, the ability to transfer CO to heme proteins, and a significant liver affinity in vivo [N1-F1]. These chemical features are important because they determine how well CO reaches its target tissues and whether the compound remains stable and usable [N1-F1].

#### b) Dosing routes and timing that matter in malaria therapy
Dosing routes and timing matter because malaria therapy often depends on precise intervention. The N4 evidence includes an example of splitting a dose of 20 mg/kg artemisinin every 24 hours into two 10 mg/kg doses every 12 hours, which was highly effective [N4-R1]. Although this is not CO-specific, it illustrates that dosing timing can influence effectiveness in malaria. In addition, the N1 evidence notes that older CO-RMs lack adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration [N1-F1], showing that formulation quality can make a major difference in whether a compound is practical and effective.

Better formulations can improve safety and efficacy, but they do not eliminate the broader safety concerns associated with CO [N3-R1][N3-R2].

---

### 4) Malaria-specific mechanisms and disease tolerance roles

CO and CORMs appear to operate through malaria-specific mechanisms that are more about disease tolerance than direct antiparasitic activity.

#### a) Roles in the heme/HO-1/CO pathway and disease tolerance
The evidence strongly supports a role for the heme/HO-1/CO pathway in malaria disease tolerance. The N2 review states that this pathway impacts the pathogenesis and outcomes of experimental severe malaria [N2-R1][N2-F2]. It also notes that HO-1 degrades heme and affects resistance and susceptibility to infection, and that heme can exert cytotoxic effects that lead to inflammation [N2-F2]. The N2-R4 excerpt adds that HO-1 and CO prevented BBB disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation, including CD8+ effects [N2-R4]. #### b) Effects on BBB disruption, neuroinflammation, and brain microvasculature

How CO and CORM chemistry and dosing shape their utility

The utility of CO and CORMs in experimental cerebral malaria is heavily shaped by their chemical design, dosing strategy, and formulation. First, CO itself is a gasotransmitter with limited bioavailability and delivery constraints, whereas CORMs are designed to overcome these by delivering CO in a controlled, localized fashion. The N1 evidence emphasizes that CO-RMs such as ALF492 enable controlled CO delivery in vivo without affecting oxygen transport by hemoglobin, a major limitation of CO inhalation therapy [N1-F1]. This chemical advantage makes CORMs more suitable for therapeutic use than gaseous CO, which is unsafe and impractical for clinical application [N1-F1].

Chemical properties also determine release and targeting. The N2 review highlights that CO-releasing molecules, mostly organometallic carbonyl complexes, are therapeutic candidates because they can deliver CO to cells and tissues in a controlled fashion [N2-F2]. The N1 study further reports that ALF492 is a novel CO-RM with improved water solubility, the ability to transfer CO to heme proteins, and a significant liver affinity in vivo [N1-F1]. These formulation differences are important because they affect bioavailability, stability, and tissue distribution after administration. In contrast, older CO-RMs like CORM-2 and CORM-3 have been noted to lack adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution, though they still serve as proof of concept [N1-F1]. This suggests that formulation improvements can enhance both safety and efficacy.

Dosing routes and timing are also central. The N4 evidence includes examples of malaria treatment strategies such as splitting a dose of 20 mg/kg artemisinin every 24 hours into two 10 mg/kg doses every 12 hours, which was highly effective [N4-R1]. While this is not directly about CO or CORMs, it illustrates the importance of dosing schedules in malaria therapy and implies that timing can influence effectiveness. The N5 evidence similarly notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids in inflammatory suppression [N5-R1], suggesting that dosing timing and combination may matter in adjunctive therapy. For CO and CORMs, the N1 evidence explicitly states that ALF492 was used as an effective adjunctive and adjuvant treatment for ECM after the onset of severe disease [N1-F1]. This indicates that dosing after disease onset may be a key consideration in malaria therapy.

Formulation differences can change safety and efficacy profiles. The N3 evidence notes that preclinical and clinical data suggest low concentrations of gaseous CO or synthetic CORMs may mitigate cellular damage, but also highlights the broader toxicity concerns associated with CO poisoning [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The N1 evidence specifically emphasizes that ALF492 does not induce measurable COHb levels in blood after in vivo administration and distributes with a significant liver affinity [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: CO and CORMs are useful because they can deliver CO in a more controlled and tissue-targeted way than gas inhalation, but their utility depends critically on chemical design, dosing route, timing, and formulation, with formulation differences able to improve safety and efficacy while still leaving toxicity risks intact [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2].

## Integrated final answer: advantages and limitations of CO and CORM adjunctive therapies in experimental cerebral malaria

Carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon monoxide-releasing molecules (CORMs) are increasingly viewed as promising adjunctive therapies in experimental cerebral malaria, but their utility is shaped by a balance of biological advantages, practical limitations, and translation barriers. The evidence from the four upstream branches points to a consistent picture: CO and CORMs are most attractive as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents rather than as direct antiparasitic treatments, and they can improve outcomes in severe malaria by protecting against neurological damage and BBB disruption. At the same time, they carry safety concerns, dose-dependent risks, and formulation-related barriers that make their clinical translation challenging [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2][N5-R1].

---

### 1) Key advantages of CO and CORMs in experimental cerebral malaria

The main advantages are mechanistic and clinical, centered on anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects.

#### a) Specific anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects
The evidence shows that CO and CORMs act through a pathway that includes heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and CO production, with documented antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immunoregulatory roles [N2-F2]. In malaria models, this pathway is especially relevant because HO-1 degrades heme and affects resistance and susceptibility to infection, while heme can exert cytotoxic effects that lead to inflammation [N2-F2]. The N1 evidence also reports that ALF492 induces HO-1 expression and that this is associated with protection in experimental cerebral malaria [N1-F1]. This is important because it suggests that CO and CORMs are not merely bystanders in malaria; they are part of a host response that actively modulates inflammation [N2-R4][N1-F1].

#### b) Improvements in clinical outcomes
The most direct clinical evidence comes from experimental cerebral malaria models. The N1 study reports that ALF492 fully protected mice against experimental cerebral malaria and acute lung injury, and that it was effective as an adjunctive and adjuvant treatment for ECM after the onset of severe disease [N1-F1]. It also found that neither HO-1 nor CO affected parasitemia, but both prevented blood-brain barrier disruption, brain microvasculature congestion, and neuroinflammation [N1-R5]. This is a critical distinction: the main benefit in malaria models appears to be reduced BBB damage and neuroinflammation, rather than lower parasite burden [N1-F1][N1-R5]. In cerebral malaria, where neurological damage is a major determinant of severity and outcome, this is a substantial advantage [N2-R4].

#### c) Potential advantages over conventional adjunctive therapies
CO and CORMs may complement rather than replace standard adjunctive therapies. The N5 evidence notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids in suppressing inflammatory effects [N5-R1], suggesting a role in augmenting conventional anti-inflammatory therapy. It also states that CO has been highlighted as a potential therapeutic agent with anti-inflammatory properties and that metal-based CORMs are emerging for their striking anti-inflammatory properties [N5-R4][N5-R3]. In that sense, CO and CORMs appear to be particularly attractive in cerebral malaria, where inflammation and BBB disruption are central pathologic features [N5-R1][N2-R4].

Overall, the advantages of CO and CORMs are best summarized as: they can reduce inflammation, protect the brain and vasculature, and may work as effective adjuncts in severe malaria, especially when administered after disease onset [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R1].

---

### 2) Major limitations and risks of CO and CORMs in experimental cerebral malaria

Despite these advantages, CO and CORMs are not without serious limitations and risks.

#### a) Toxicity and safety concerns
CO itself is a poison, and CO poisoning can have serious clinical consequences ranging from headache and dizziness to coma and death [N3-R2]. The N3 evidence also notes that preclinical and clinical data suggest low concentrations of gaseous CO or synthetic CORMs may mitigate cellular damage, but it also highlights the broader toxicity concerns associated with CO poisoning [N3-R1][N3-R2]. This is a major limitation because it means that even if CO is beneficial in malaria, its use must be carefully controlled to avoid systemic toxicity [N3-R2].

#### b) Dose-dependent adverse effects and variability across species or models
The evidence suggests that efficacy and safety are dose-dependent. The N1 study notes that substantial protective effects similar to CO inhalation have been reported using CORMs, but that these CO-RMs lack some key drug-like properties, including adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration [N1-F1]. The N4 evidence provides an example of dose splitting in malaria treatment, showing that splitting a 20 mg/kg dose into two 10 mg/kg doses every 12 hours was highly effective [N4-R1]. While this is not CO-specific, it illustrates the importance of timing and dosing in malaria therapy and implies that different models or species may respond differently to CO or CORM exposure [N4-R1]. The N5 evidence also notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids, which suggests that the interaction between dose, timing, and adjunctive therapy can change the overall effect [N5-R1].

#### c) Barriers to translation: delivery, stability, and pharmacokinetics
One of the major barriers to clinical translation is that CO gas therapy remains unsafe and requires highly controlled medical facilities [N1-F1]. CORMs were developed precisely to overcome this limitation by delivering CO in a controlled, localized way [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, older CO-RMs such as CORM-2 and CORM-3 have been noted to lack adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration [N1-F1]. This means that formulation differences can significantly affect whether a CORM behaves like a useful therapeutic or a problematic compound [N1-F1]. The N3 evidence also reinforces the broader safety concern by emphasizing that CO poisoning can be fatal [N3-R3].

In short, the limitations are: toxicity, dose dependence, formulation instability, and the challenge of translating a gas-based therapy into a safe and practical clinical intervention [N3-R2][N1-F1][N4-R1].

---

### 3) How CO and CORM chemistry and dosing shape their utility

The utility of CO and CORMs is strongly shaped by their chemistry, dosing strategy, and formulation.

#### a) Chemical properties affecting bioavailability and release
CO itself is a gasotransmitter with limited bioavailability and delivery constraints, whereas CORMs are designed to overcome these by delivering CO in a controlled, localized fashion [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The N2 review explains that CO-releasing molecules, mostly organometallic carbonyl complexes, are therapeutic candidates because they can deliver CO to cells and tissues in a controlled fashion [N2-F2]. The N1 evidence reports that ALF492 is a novel CO-RM with improved water solubility, the ability to transfer CO to heme proteins, and a significant liver affinity in vivo [N1-F1]. These chemical features are important because they determine how well CO reaches its target tissues and whether the compound remains stable and usable [N1-F1].

#### b) Dosing routes and timing that matter in malaria therapy
Dosing routes and timing matter because malaria therapy often depends on precise intervention. The N4 evidence includes an example of splitting a dose of 20 mg/kg artemisinin every 24 hours into two 10 mg/kg doses every 12 hours, which was highly effective [N4-R1]. Although this is not CO-specific, it illustrates that dosing timing can influence effectiveness in malaria. The N5 evidence also notes that CO can potentiate corticosteroids in suppressing inflammatory effects, which further suggests that timing and combination matter [N5-R1]. For CO and CORMs, the N1 evidence explicitly states that ALF492 was used as an effective adjunctive and adjuvant treatment for ECM after the onset of severe disease [N1-F1]. This suggests that dosing after disease onset may be a key consideration in malaria therapy [N1-F1].

This formulation distinction reduces some of the limitations of CO gas and may improve safety. However, the N3 evidence also reminds us that CO poisoning can have serious clinical consequences, ranging from headache and dizziness to coma and death [N3-R2]. In addition, the N1 evidence notes that older CO-RMs lack adequate solubility, stability, and tissue distribution after administration [N1-F1], showing that formulation quality can make a major difference in whether a compound is practical and effective.

In summary, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: CO and CORMs are useful because they can deliver CO in a more controlled and tissue-targeted way than gas inhalation, but their utility depends critically on chemical design, dosing route, timing, and formulation [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2]. Better formulations can improve safety and efficacy, but they do not eliminate the broader safety concerns associated with CO [N3-R1][N3-R2].
